item.research_question: How can non-equiatomic medium-entropy alloys be designed to achieve novel two-phase microstructures, and can existing parametric phase formation rules predict the phase separation behaviors in these alloys?
item.processing_route: Vacuum arc-melting under argon protection with electromagnetic stirring five times, followed by natural cooling in the furnace
item.test_conditions: Room temperature characterization using X-ray diffractometer (Cu radiation, 2θ: 20°–100°), scanning electron microscopy, and transmission electron microscopy with high-angle annular dark-field detector and energy dispersive spectrometry
key_findings: The alloys exhibit novel two-phase microstructures consisting of B2-ordered nanoprecipitates and BCC-disordered matrix.
As the Fe content (x) increases from 25 to 65, the nanoprecipitate structure transfers from a spinodal-like intertwined structure to a nanoparticle dispersed structure.
In the Fe25 alloy, the Ni-Al-rich and Fe-Cr-rich phases alternate with a period of about 200 nm in width.
The average size of nanoparticles decreases with increasing Fe content: ~400 nm in Fe35, ~250 nm in Fe45, ~200 nm in Fe55, and ~100 nm in Fe65.
The Fe55 and Fe65 alloys contain a large density of highly dispersed nanoparticles in the matrix.

Previous parametric approaches (atomic size difference δ, mixing enthalpy ΔHmix, mixing entropy ΔSmix, valence electron concentration VEC, and parameter Ω) are unable to describe the phase separation behaviors observed.
The VEC values for the alloys range between 6.75 and 7.42, yet only BCC and B2 phases form, contradicting the VEC rule that predicts FCC phase stability for VEC ≥ 8.
item.mechanism: Phase separation is driven by thermodynamic factors where Ni and Al have the most negative mixing enthalpy and largest electronegativity difference, favoring the formation of Ni-Al-rich B2 phases; Fe is thermodynamically favored to dissolve in the B2 phase, while Cr stays in the matrix forming the BCC phase due to smaller electronegativity difference with Al. The morphology (intertwined vs. dispersed) is controlled by the concentration of Ni and Al elements.
item.limitations: The detailed formation processes of the Ni-Al-rich precipitates in the Fex(CrNiAl)100−x alloys are still unclear.
item.future_work: The detailed formation processes of the Ni-Al-rich precipitates will be studied in the future.
quotes: Here we propose a novel design of non-equiatomic medium-entropy alloys that contain one matrix element and several equiatomic alloying elements.
Detailed characterization reveals that the alloys exhibit novel two-phase microstructures consisting of B2-ordered nanoprecipitates and BCC-disordered matrix.
Previous parametric approaches to predict phase formation rules for high-entropy alloys are unable to describe the phase separation behaviors in the studied alloys.
